summary:
Marswalk is a planner and in-suit copilot for astronauts walking on Mars. A message to Earth takes many minutes, but dust devils, storms and solar particle events change in seconds, so the crew can't wait for help from Earth.

We built a 10 × 10 km terrain model of Jezero Crater from NASA and USGS data and checked it against 306 positions of the Perseverance rover. In the habitat, the astronaut plans the walk on a 3D map. The route avoids steep slopes, cliffs and soft sand, within the limits of oxygen, daylight and radiation. A phone shows a first-person preview of the path. During the walk, a watch guides the astronaut home. The copilot predicts where moving hazards will be and decides whether to continue, reroute, wait, return or take shelter. Every decision is deterministic and checked by a safety validator. An AI only explains the decision in plain words; it never makes it. After each walk, the system prints a one-page Survival Guide.

This turns orbital data into a practical, personal survival guide. We tested it in 1,152 simulated walks on real Jezero terrain, using hazard values measured by NASA missions. With the copilot, 99.7% of astronauts returned alive, compared with 87% without it. On long routes the gap was 99% vs 70%.
details:
What it does and how it works
Marswalk Copilot plans and guides astronaut walks on Mars, and keeps guiding them when conditions change. It has three parts:

  • Planner (in the habitat): the astronaut picks stops on a 3D map of a 10 × 10 km area of Jezero Crater. The planner finds a route that avoids steep slopes, cliffs and rough terrain. It also checks that the walk fits the oxygen budget, the safety reserve and the daylight left.
  • Phone: shows a first-person preview of the route before the walk.
  • Watch: stays with the astronaut for the whole walk. One needle points home and the other follows the route. When a hazard appears, the screen flashes DANGER with the copilot's instruction and the reason for it.

When a hazard appears (dust storm, marsquake rockfall, solar particle event, suit leak or fatigue), the copilot recomputes oxygen, time and risk for the rest of the walk. It then decides: continue, reroute, wait, return now, or emergency. Every decision comes from fixed rules in the code, so the same situation always gets the same answer. A small language model running locally only explains the decision in plain words. It cannot change it.

Benefits
In a reproducible benchmark on real Jezero terrain, we simulated 1,152 walks, each with one to three random hazards:

  • Survival: with the copilot, 99.7% of astronauts came home. Walking the shortest route without it, 87% did. On walks longer than 5 km: 99% versus 70%.
  • Fully safe walks: home before dusk without touching the oxygen reserve rose from 57% to 89%.
  • Never worse: there was no walk where the copilot made the outcome worse.

Intended impact

  • Mars: crews on Mars cannot wait many minutes for advice from Earth. Marswalk Copilot gives them a deterministic decision they can check, on the spot.
  • Training: crews can rehearse walks and hazards on real terrain before a mission.
  • Earth: the same engine could support mountain rescue teams and remote field work.

Tools and technologies

  • Data:
    • Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter CTX and HiRISE elevation models (USGS), fetched through STAC.
    • Map checked against 306 Perseverance rover positions.
    • Hazard values from published NASA mission data: Perseverance MEDA, Curiosity RAD, InSight, Apollo metabolic rates.
  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, NumPy, Google OR-Tools.
  • Explanations: local language model through Ollama.
  • Frontend: React, Vite, three.js for the 3D terrain, React Router, packaged as a desktop app with Electron.
  • Benchmark: Node.js, with a fixed random seed.
  • Hardware: none special; the phone and watch screens are simulated in the app.

What makes it creative

  • It uses the logic of aviation software: a simulator to train on and a cockpit-style copilot that gives one clear instruction.
  • It treats hazards as moving: the copilot predicts where a hazard will be, not just where it is now.
  • It splits the work across three devices, each matching what the astronaut needs at that moment of the walk.
  • It is AI-assisted without trusting AI with life-or-death decisions.

Factors we considered

  • Safety first: a validator removes every unsafe option, and a fixed rule picks the safest one left.
  • Reproducibility: fixed seeds, same results on every run.
  • Honest data: real terrain and cited sources, with every assumption listed.
  • Explainability: every decision comes with its reason.
  • Communication delay with Earth.
  • Usability under stress: big warnings, minimal reading.
